content: Obeticholic acid is indicated for the treatment of primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) in adults without cirrhosis or with compensated cirrhosis, provided there is no evidence of portal hypertension. It can be used in combination with ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) in patients who have had an inadequate response to UDCA for at least one year or as monotherapy in patients who are intolerant to UDCA. The safety and efficacy of obeticholic acid have not been established in all populations. While no overall differences in safety or effectiveness were observed in patients older than 65 years, some older individuals may exhibit increased sensitivity. Cholestyramine, colesevelam, and colestipol can reduce the levels or effects of obeticholic acid by binding to the drug in the gastrointestinal tract. To mitigate this interaction, obeticholic acid should be administered at least four hours before or four hours after taking bile acid-binding resins. Additionally, obeticholic acid can increase the levels or effects of drugs metabolized by the hepatic enzyme CYP1A2, such as theophylline and tizanidine. Close monitoring is recommended for CYP1A2 substrates with a narrow therapeutic index, and dose adjustments may be necessary. Common side effects of obeticholic acid include pruritus (56–70%), fatigue (19–25%), severe pruritus (19–23%), reduced HDL-C levels (9–20%), abdominal pain and discomfort (10–19%), rash (7–10%), arthralgia (6–10%), oropharyngeal pain (7–8%), dizziness (7%), constipation (7%), peripheral edema (3–7%), palpitations (3–7%), pyrexia (7%), thyroid function abnormalities (4–6%), and eczema (3–6%). Hepatobiliary disorders, such as liver failure, new-onset cirrhosis, increased bilirubin levels, and worsening jaundice, have also been reported. Obeticholic acid is contraindicated in patients with complete biliary obstruction, decompensated cirrhosis (e.g., Child-Pugh Class B or C), or a history of decompensation events. Patients with compensated cirrhosis and evidence of portal hypertension (e.g., ascites, gastroesophageal varices, or persistent thrombocytopenia) should also avoid this medication. Patients with PBC often exhibit hyperlipidemia characterized by elevated total cholesterol, primarily due to increased HDL-C levels. Monitoring for reductions in HDL-C is recommended. For patients who do not respond to the highest tolerated dose of obeticholic acid (10 mg/day) after one year and experience a reduction in HDL-C, the risks and benefits of continuing treatment should be carefully weighed. Severe pruritus has been reported, and patients with new or worsening pruritus should be evaluated. Management strategies may include bile acid-binding resins, antihistamines, dose reduction, or temporary dose interruption. There is limited human data on the use of obeticholic acid during pregnancy, and the available information is insufficient to determine drug-associated risks. Similarly, there is no information on the presence of obeticholic acid in human milk, its effects on breastfed infants, or its impact on milk production. When considering the use of obeticholic acid in breastfeeding mothers, the developmental and health benefits of breastfeeding should be weighed against the mother’s clinical need for the drug and any potential adverse effects on the infant. Obeticholic acid is a farnesoid X receptor (FXR) agonist. FXR is a nuclear receptor expressed in the liver, intestine, kidney, and adipose tissue that regulates genes involved in bile acid synthesis and transport, lipid metabolism, and glucose homeostasis. Obeticholic acid is highly protein-bound (>99%) and has a volume of distribution of 618 liters. It is conjugated with glycine or taurine in the liver and secreted into bile. These conjugates are either reabsorbed in the small intestine for enterohepatic recirculation or excreted in feces. Approximately 87% of the drug is excreted in feces, with less than 3% excreted in urine. Obeticholic acid can be taken with or without food. When co-administered with bile acid-binding resins, the doses should be separated by at least four hours or as long an interval as possible. The medication should be stored at 20–25°C (68–77°F), with permissible excursions to 15–30°C (59–86°F). This information is provided for general educational purposes and may vary depending on individual circumstances. For the most current and specific information, consult the applicable healthcare provider or plan provider.
